description:
The Sikorsky S-55, known to US forces as the H-19 Chickasaw, was the first helicopter built around a proper troop and cargo cabin rather than seats bolted to a frame. Designed under Edward Katzenberger for transport, casualty evacuation and rescue, it first flew on 10 November 1949.

It carried troops and wounded in Korea and served the US Army, Air Force, Navy (HO4S), Marines (HRS) and Coast Guard, plus many export air arms. It was also licence-built by Westland in Britain, SNCASE in France and Mitsubishi in Japan; about 1,728 were completed in all, 1,281 of them by Sikorsky. Westland's Whirlwind was progressively re-engined, finally with a Gnome turboshaft in the HAR.9, HAR.10 and civil Series 3, and those turbine machines flew rescue sorties into the early 1980s.

Stand at the nose and the layout explains itself: clamshell doors swing open to expose the engine mounted in the nose, so mechanics work at chest height. With the engine low and forward, the cabin sits above and behind it, and the drive shaft runs up at a steep angle between the two pilots, who perch in a glazed box above. That freed a square, unobstructed cabin under the rotor for ten troops or eight stretchers.
engines: 1 x Pratt & Whitney R-1340-57 Wasp 9-cylinder radial, 600 hp

description:
The Beechcraft Model 18 was a twin-engined light transport built to carry six to eleven people faster and farther than the single-engine aircraft feeder airlines and businesses then used. Designed at Beech Aircraft in Wichita under Walter Beech and chief engineer Ted Wells, it first flew on 15 January 1937.

War turned it into a trainer. The USAAF and Navy bought it as the C-45 Expeditor utility transport, the AT-7 Navigator, the AT-11 Kansan bombing and gunnery trainer, and the Navy SNB series; most American bombardiers and navigators trained in one. Around 9,000 were built in all civil and military forms between 1937 and 1969, and many still fly as freighters, warbirds and skydiving aircraft.

Standing in front of one, look for the twin fins on the tailplane, the radial engines slung under a low wing, and the nose-high taildragger stance on tall main gear. An AT-11 is easy to pick out: its nose is a framed glass bombardier station instead of solid metal, and it has a bomb bay in the belly. That tough, easily rebuilt airframe kept the type in production for 32 years.
engines: 2 x Pratt & Whitney R-985 Wasp Junior radial, 450 hp each
source_name: National Museum of the United States Air Force — Beech C-45H Expeditor

description:
The Stearman Model 75 is the biplane on which wartime America learned to fly: a rugged primary trainer, first flown on 1 January 1934, as the Army and Navy expanded pilot training. Stearman became a Boeing subsidiary that same year, so it is known as Stearman, Boeing Stearman or Kaydet.

Army and Navy flew one aeroplane under different names, differing mainly in engine — the PT-13 has a Lycoming R-680, the PT-17 a Continental R-670, and the Navy's N2S covered both, in the yellow that earned the nickname Yellow Peril. At least 10,626 were built across the Model 70, 75 and 76 family, a total that includes airframes delivered as spare parts. Thousands went cheaply to civilians after 1945, many as crop dusters, and some air forces flew them into the 1960s.

Notice the tandem open cockpits, instructor behind pupil, and the bare cylinders of an uncowled radial. Then look at the landing gear: wide, stiffly sprung legs kept it planted on rough grass, yet a tall stance and light tail let it swap ends in a ground loop if a student was lazy with the rudder. Forgiving in the air, unforgiving on the ground — the lesson a beginner needed.
engines: 1 x Continental R-670-5 7-cylinder air-cooled radial, 220 hp
source_name: Wikipedia, Boeing-Stearman Model 75 — Specifications (PT-17), after Bowers 1989

description:
The Chipmunk was the first aircraft designed entirely by de Havilland Canada, drawn up at Downsview by the Polish engineer Wsiewolod Jakimiuk to replace the Tiger Moth biplane on which Commonwealth air forces had learned to fly. It first flew on 22 May 1946, an all-metal low-wing monoplane with an enclosed cockpit, a forgiving stall and honest aerobatic manners.

Canada built 217, but the type's career was largely European. Britain licence-built about 1,000 at Hatfield and Chester, 735 of them as the RAF's Chipmunk T.10, and OGMA at Alverca assembled 66 for Portugal — a combined Canadian, British and Portuguese total of about 1,283. Chipmunks trained RCAF and RAF pupils, equipped University Air Squadrons and gave Air Training Corps cadets their first flight; the last RAF examples left the Air Experience Flights in 1996.

Standing in front of one, look for the long glazed canopy over two tandem seats, the gently tapered low wing, and the slim nose of the inverted Gipsy Major. A generation of RAF pilots, Prince Philip among them, flew their first solo from this cockpit.
engines: 1 x de Havilland Gipsy Major 1C 4-cylinder inverted inline, 145 hp
source_name: Wikipedia, de Havilland Canada DHC-1 Chipmunk — Specifications (DHC-1 Chipmunk)

description:
The OH-58 began as a loser. Bell's entry in the US Army's early-1960s light observation helicopter contest was beaten by the Hughes OH-6. Bell reworked the losing design into a sleek five-seat civil machine, the Model 206A JetRanger, flown in 1966. When the Army reopened the contest in 1967, Bell offered the JetRanger, underbid Hughes and won it as the OH-58A Kiowa.

Kiowas reached Vietnam in 1969, scouting at treetop height ahead of gunships. The armed OH-58D Kiowa Warrior added a mast-mounted sight — a ball above the rotor letting the crew watch a target while the aircraft stayed hidden; the Army withdrew the type from front-line service in 2017. Agusta built it under licence in Italy, and civil JetRangers became the standard police, news and air-taxi machine worldwide. Some 7,300 were built across all civil 206 and military OH-58 versions.

Up close it is small and plain. The main rotor has just two long blades on a teetering hub, which give it a loping beat in flight. The tailboom is slim, the cabin a glassy bubble with a scout's downward view. Few shapes account for more of the world's helicopter hours.
source_name: Pima Air & Space Museum — Bell OH-58A

description:
The Sea King was the first helicopter able to hunt a submarine and kill it in one airframe. Sikorsky built it around a boat-shaped amphibious hull, twin turboshafts for safety over open sea, and enough lift to carry dipping sonar and torpedoes together — work that had needed two aircraft. It first flew in March 1959.

US Navy Sea Kings hunted submarines from carrier decks and recovered the Apollo astronauts. Westland built it under licence at Yeovil from 1969, re-engined with Rolls-Royce Gnome turboshafts and given British radar and sonar; those machines flew anti-submarine and commando sorties in the Falklands and decades of Navy and RAF search and rescue. The Commando, or HC.4, was a land-based troop carrier without the boat hull and sponsons. Some 1,300 came from Sikorsky, Westland, Agusta and Mitsubishi together.

Look underneath first: the belly is a boat, with stub sponsons carrying the mainwheels that steady it afloat. The five-blade main rotor and the tail fold for stowage aboard ship. And it is simply large — nearly 19 m across the rotor disc — dwarfing the light helicopters beside it.
engines: 2 x Rolls-Royce Gnome H.1400-2 turboshaft, 1,660 shp each
source_name: Wikipedia, Westland Sea King — Specifications (Sea King HAS.5)
